title: In 1999, Florida began restoring the Kissimmee River, a project that aims to reconnect 44 miles of channel and restore 20,000 acres of wetlands | Hindustan Times
text:
Why a straight river was a problem
The canal reduced flooding, but it came with a cost that no one planned for. It cut the river off from its floodplain, destroying wetlands and damaging the ecosystem along the river. Birds, fish, and other wildlife dependent on those wetlands began to decline. The concept of restoring the river first arose in 1976. Congress authorized the project in the Water Resources Development Act of 1992. Then, in 1994, the South Florida Water Management District and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers agreed to share the cost equally. The aim was to fill in 22 miles of the C-38 canal and reconnect 44 miles of river channel so water could flow more as it did in the past.
